description: We develop an interactive web platform and educational games to rigorously test ocean trends and the potential connection between the Southern Ocean and the Peruvian upwelling (anchoveta ecosystem). By integrating satellite data into 3D maps, we make complex statistical analysis accessible. We seek collaborators in programming (React/Python), oceanography, data analysis, ecological modeling, and digital design.
summary:
Chaski Polar is an interactive educational platform built around the research question: “Is the Southern Ocean Connected to Peru’s Upwelling System? Testing Ocean Trends and Long-Lag Associations, 1998–2025.”

It turns complex oceanographic and fisheries data into an accessible experience. Through a 3D globe, satellite visualizations, a trend tester, guided tours, species cards, and educational games, students, educators, and curious users observe ocean changes, compare variables and periods, and learn to interpret trends and uncertainty.

Integrating open data from NASA, ESA, NOAA, NSIDC, Copernicus, FAO, IMARPE, and BCRP, Chaski Polar encourages users to explore real observations and ask whether a trend is consistent or sensitive to the timeframe.

The platform also presents anchoveta ecosystem and fishery context for coastal communities. A plain-language comparison tool for small-scale fishers is planned; it does not currently issue operational fishing alerts, identify fishing windows automatically, or provide catch forecasts.

Its goal is to strengthen data literacy and critical understanding of ocean change through direct interaction with real scientific evidence.
details:
Chaski Polar: Exploring Ocean Change Through Real Data

What does the project do, and how does it work?

Chaski Polar is an open, interactive educational platform built around the research question: “Is the Southern Ocean Connected to Peru’s Upwelling System? Testing Ocean Trends and Long-Lag Associations, 1998–2025.”

The platform transforms complex oceanographic and fisheries data into an accessible learning experience. Through an interactive 3D globe, satellite data visualizations, a trend tester, guided tours, species cards, and two educational games, users can explore variables such as sea surface temperature, chlorophyll-a, sea level, sea ice, oxygen, nutrients, El Niño signals, anchoveta landings, and fishery ecosystem context.

The core idea is that users do not simply look at maps — they actively test trends. They can choose a variable, a region, a data source, and a time period, and then see how the result changes when they adjust the start year, exclude extreme El Niño years, or compare two satellite sources. This hands-on interaction helps users understand that a trend can be consistent, fragile, or dependent on the timeframe, and that a null result is also scientific evidence.

What benefits does it offer?

  • Students and educators: A practical, visual example of how a scientific trend is tested, and why a trend may disappear depending on the selected period. It supports data literacy and critical thinking.
  • Early-career analysts and citizen scientists: Open code, documented methods, and downloadable tables allow them to reproduce and verify the analysis.
  • Researchers and agencies working on the Humboldt system: A transparent baseline of what 28 years of satellite and reanalysis data can and cannot show about a Southern Ocean link.
  • Coastal and fishing communities: Oceanographic and anchoveta ecosystem information presented in plain language, helping users understand how environmental conditions relate to fishery records. A plain-language comparison tool for small-scale fishers is planned as future work.

What is the intended impact?

The expected impact is educational and focused on data literacy. Chaski Polar aims to help people develop a critical understanding of ocean change by interacting directly with real scientific evidence. It encourages users to distinguish between consistent trends and fragile signals, and to recognize the limits of available data.

The project also seeks to bring ocean and fisheries information closer to coastal communities as an informational audience. However, it does not currently issue operational fishing alerts, automatically identify fishing windows, or provide catch forecasts. It is not an operational fishing aid and has not been validated with fishers.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software were used?

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, R, HTML, CSS.
  • Web frameworks and libraries: React 19, Vite, Three.js, react-globe.gl, Recharts, Tailwind CSS (light use), zustand, zod.
  • Data processing and analysis: NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, xarray, netCDF4, rasterio, matplotlib, and the Copernicus Marine and NASA client libraries.
  • Visualization: Interactive 3D globe, per-cell maps, time-series and bar charts, and 3D scenes built with Three.js.
  • Character and graphic assets: The main game uses pixel-art characters drawn in code on a canvas. The pre-event game used Aseprite for sprites and Blender for 3D models.
  • Web development and hosting: Git and GitHub, pnpm, Vite, oxlint, Node.js for verification scripts, and Vercel for hosting.
  • Hardware: No specific hardware is required. Heavy processing runs offline on servers, while trend calculations run in the user’s browser.

In what sense is the project creative?

Chaski Polar’s creativity lies in turning a complex scientific question into an interactive and playful experience. It does not stop at showing visualizations — it invites users to “play” with the data: changing the start year, excluding extreme El Niño years, or comparing two satellite sources to see how the answer changes.

The platform also integrates two educational games. In Cardumen: the anchoveta saga, the player guides an anchoveta school through six real years, with food availability following real satellite chlorophyll data and the oxygen-poor layer sinking during El Niño. In From Ice to Anchovy, the player reads Antarctic and Peruvian signals and guesses whether anchoveta or scallop landings rose or fell. Both games reinforce the scientific objective through exploration and decision-making.

Games and Gameplay

The project includes two educational games that reinforce the scientific objective through exploration and decision-making.

  • Cardumen: The Anchoveta Saga: The player starts with a prologue featuring three characters (phytoplankton, krill, and a humpback whale) that illustrates the Antarctic–Peru connection through migrating animals. Then, the player guides an anchoveta school through six real years (2004, 1998, 2000, 2017, 2023, 2026). Food availability in each zone follows the real satellite chlorophyll of that month; the oxygen-poor layer sinks during El Niño, and predators and fishing fleets are present. Between years, a desk scene asks the player to cross-check a satellite report with documents, press notes (some with false figures), and causal claims, classify the year (El Niño, normal, variability, or trend), and choose a strategy for the next generation. The school sizes, losses, and strategies are illustrative; the sea is real.

  • From Ice to Anchovy: A pixel-art game of eight rounds, each a real year between 1999 and 2024. The player spends 14 hours of satellite time reading signals (four from Antarctica, three from Peru), then guesses whether Peruvian anchoveta or scallop landings rose or fell and chooses a confidence level. The reveal shows FAO landings and which signals helped. The final chart shows, as an association, that Peruvian coastal signals relate to landings and Antarctic ones barely do. It is available in English and linked from the temperature panel.

Both games use real data but present their mechanics as educational illustrations. They do not feed results back into the analysis.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Scientific rigor and transparency: More than 2,300 documented statistical tests, including null and fragile results, are reported as part of the evidence. False-discovery-rate correction, start-year sensitivity, and source comparison are applied and explained.
  • Accessibility and education: Plain-language definitions, “Read this as” sentences, guided tours, and educational games make the content accessible to non-specialists.
  • Honesty about limits: The project explicitly states what it does not do — it does not predict catches, does not issue operational fishing alerts, and does not prove causation. It clearly separates what is implemented from what is planned as future work.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

In Chaski Polar, AI tools were used as development and research assistants. All AI-generated content, code, and text were rigorously reviewed, validated, and adapted by the human team to ensure scientific accuracy and data integrity.

AI as a Development Tool:

  • Claude Code (Anthropic): Assisted in writing and refactoring web code and analysis scripts, debugging, running browser tests for the games, and drafting technical documentation. It also supported the creation of the pre-event game, which was later adapted and integrated into the site.
  • Codex (OpenAI): Provided implementation guidance, helped structure web and analysis code, and assisted in debugging verification scripts.
  • AI Image Generation: Used to generate a conceptual mock-up of the landing page featuring a whale. (Note: This image was strictly for design brainstorming, is not in the repository, and was not used as a final deliverable).
  • Large Language Models (LLMs): Assisted in drafting plain-language interface texts (e.g., the "Read this as" sections) and translating game narratives into English.
